utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Piletta-Zanin to address the Chamber and I understood that Mr. Ierace also wanted to address the Chamber, I'll perhaps first deal with the exhibits of yesterday -- I should say the documents tendered. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. What I wanted to say was -- should be chronologically before we go on to the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, what we wanted to state so that it appears properly in the transcript, we still believe that the hearing of this expert witness, Dr. Kovacs, should not have happened -- would not have happened because looking at the procedure, the way that it happened, the Defence never received original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... What you told us before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what I wanted to say was that procedurally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... If you address this Chamber with a certain issue, we'll listen carefully. And it's not necessary to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. But I'm not repeating. It's just that officially now, formally, for the motives aforementioned, we want to place certification for appeal because this is something we haven't done before. I don't want to take too much time, but we want to formally ask for certification of appeal in accordance with Rule 73(B) so that we can explain in writing next week. I think the delay would be expected because it was on Saturday that we found out that you have asked for a new appearance by expert witness Kovacs. So this is why we're asking for certification of appeal in accordance with Rule 73(B). And we would like to do it in writing. No one will waste any time. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The decision that the Prosecution would be allowed to re-call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I wanted to explain. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we'll deal with the documents. Madam Registrar, could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3725A, report; Exhibit P3725A.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to the report, we object to the tendering of this document. The reasons why we object to it are the following: The conditions under which this report was written seem extraordinary, and also it seem that this witness has simply lied when he was examined in court yesterday. I don't think in any case we should accept the admission into evidence of this report since they are the result of manipulations. I have to remind you, first of all, that the witness said that -- that there was a date that was wrong and he said that there were missing pages in the report. There was a lot of confusion, and this should not be acceptable and it should not be accepted. Furthermore, the Defence still hasn't had time to check each one of the pages of this report, and therefore provisionally we cannot treat this document as admissible. And in essence, the way and the conditions under which the report was established, this is in opposition to the Rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber will decide in due course on the objection. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D166, excerpt from report in Hungarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No objection really; however, it was read out in evidence and was fully ventilated in court. I don't know if we want to over-flood the record with unnecessary documents. But we have no objections to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the whole text you submitted to the witness has been read and the parties agreed that this was part of the report. Is there any specific need why -- but if you insist, we -- there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I think that in this case, it would be useful for your Chamber to see visually the differences in the text. The official difference, formal difference, even if there is a language barrier, I think that this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is admitted. Madam Registrar, no further documents?. Then -- Mr. Ierace, you wanted to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, two matters, one for closed session and the other for open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then first turn into closed session if that's your following order. Could we do with private session, because that would save us closing off seven curtains.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't recall the distinction, Mr. President. I'd be grateful if you could remind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, everyone can still see us but not hear us any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me turn not into closed session but into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to examine this, but until when? What I mean is when would you like us to intervene on this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the Chamber will do is to read this document during the first break. And then of course we can identify -- but now we are dealing in open session with an issue. I would say during the first break we'll try to understand what it is. If the Defence could do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would appreciate that. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution is in considerable difficulty in finishing its case by next Friday. As matters stand at the moment, we have some nine witnesses left to call in six hearing days. The factors which have contributed to this situation are more than one. At this stage, unless you wish otherwise, I won't go into those factors. Wherever blame lies for those factors, the end result is that the Prosecution and the Prosecution alone pays the price. Whoever is responsible for the delays, that time inevitably comes off what time the Prosecution has to complete its case. Mr. President, one simple remedy in part, although not in full, would be if it was possible for us to sit longer next week, perhaps starting earlier and sitting later. I understand, for instance, that the trial that normally takes place in this Trial Chamber will not sit again for four weeks. Mr. President, there are other steps that perhaps can be taken. And of course there is the usual step, that the Prosecution cuts its own case. In relation to the evidence that the Prosecution sought to lead from Zoran Lesic, for instance, I indicated two days ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, if I may interrupt you. If you are finished with what you are telling us, it was my intention to give two oral decisions. And perhaps it might assist you if you knew already about them by now. There is a suggestion, at least, made by the Prosecution to re-call the witness Philipps in respect of what I call the GPS issue. That request will be denied. Then there is another request, which would be to re-call Mr. Lesic, in respect of markings on the map. So I'm not talking about a 92 bis Lesic statement but I am talking about re-call of Lesic in view of these maps. That request will be denied as well. So if that would influence what you're going to tell us, but at least that you know -- I'll give you the reasons after you've finished, unless you would like to know them now. Then I could first start to give these decisions in more detail and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that the Defence filed some argument in relation to our request to re-call Mr. Lesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the Prosecution did not have an opportunity to respond to that. I also note that it leaves the Prosecution in this position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Ierace, of course there is always an possibility that the Chamber will reconsider decisions. But we received many, many, many requests just very shortly before the conclusion of the presentation of the Prosecution's case. And we have to take decisions. I mean, I don't think that the Prosecution would have been very happy if we would have come with these decisions next Friday at 2.00. But perhaps if you say, well, I could give the decisions later on, then I'll first let you continue. If you say, "No, I'd rather hear now the reasons also why," then I could give you the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if you are able to give the reasons as to why Mr. Lesic is not permitted, or rather, as to why the Prosecution is not permitted to call Mr. Lesic to confirm the positions of the victims when hit, I would be grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Because it may be of assistance to the Prosecution in reformulating its evidence in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The reason for not to allow the Prosecution to re-call Mr. Lesic for the reasons given is that the evidence as it is now, that is, a lot of maps, videos, 360-degrees photographs, oral testimony, et cetera, is in the view of the Chamber sufficient to enable the Chamber to make the determination of where the victims were when there was an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. impact. So whether someone -- I mean, if we would have a blank map, we could almost put the dots on them ourselves. Apart from that, there's of course -- and that cannot be changed by Mr. Lesic -- whenever there has been any dispute about whether the witness was left of the pedestrian crossings or to the right of the pedestrian crossings, of course a dot on the map could not resolve that issue. So therefore, where there is anything in dispute, it cannot be cured in whatever way by pointing at red dots on maps. And where it's not in dispute, it's -- it's no trouble for the Chamber to locate the -- the places where the victims were. And more or less the same is true for the re-call of Mr. Philipps. GPS, if there were any mistakes, until now no one has ever talked about the GPS any more. And the GPS locations could not resolve any dispute - there were hardly any, but there were a few - and that could not be resolved by GPS. So what we are doing is a very -- what the Prosecution invites the Chamber to do is to make a lot of effort to change a few numbers which have not been in dispute at this moment, which have not been used by anyone up till this moment. So as it stands now - and of course I have to stress that - as it stands now, also taking into consideration the position the Defence has taken up to this moment on these issues, there is no need to hear that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that -- I'm grateful for the opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps I'll finish one thing because then you have the whole reasons why. Since the Prosecution has informed the Chamber that the GPS figures are incorrect, we'll ignore them. And since it has been indicated that there might be other incorrect figures as well in the statement of Mr. Lesic, the Chamber would like to know what other entries in that statement are incorrect so that we can see whether there's any need to have them corrected or that we also just ignore them. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you wish, I can do that now, Mr. President, or later, at your convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps if -- if it could be written down. It takes a lot of time in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- oh, yes, and perhaps finally I could tell you that there's another request pending. That is the 92 bis request in respect of Mr. Lesic. That takes us more time. We would have expected -- the Chamber would have expected that the Prosecution would not have just indicated what documents these were but also when tendered, whether there were any objections or not, because that's what we have to find out anyhow before we can give a decision. And that's a lot of work. So the Lesic 92 bis statement request, at this moment I cannot give you a decision on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to that last observation, do you mean by that to refer to the opening video segments? Because if that is the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there's a long list of all kind of photographs, and it's not just a video but there's a lot -- a lot of information attached to these statements that for each location, at what time the photograph was taken, and from - but it's - these are long lists with exhibit numbers, and it's not clear for all of them whether there will ever be any objection to the admission into evidence and whether they were finally admitted. So we'll have to check all that. And we, as a matter of fact, would have expected the Prosecution to provide that information immediately so that it would save time and that we could give a quicker decision. But let's not discuss this at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As you please, Mr. President. Given what you've just said, I won't take it any further. Well, thank you, Mr. President. That's essentially my request, that if it's possible for us to expand the sitting hours next week, that would be of great assistance to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that. But first, of course, if we're willing to do so have to we'll have to inquire any possibilities to that. Could you -- having -- knowing now what the decisions are in respect of Mr. Philipps and Mr. Lesic, as far as the re-call is concerned, could you give us some indication on how much time you would need for -- would that be nine witnesses or would that be seven?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That would now be seven. And frustratingly we are now unable to advance any of our witnesses into Monday. We are left with only Mr. Gavrankapetanovic on Monday. I have also -- with that in mind, I have also provided to the Defence yesterday evening a table of exhibits which the Prosecution proposes to tender directly from the bar table. Those exhibits comprise -- I think it's 17 documents and one video cassette. Copies of those documents will be provided to the Defence by today to assist them in coming to terms with the contents. I can indicate that they are either official UN documents or VRS documents. And having regard to the policy of the Registry in relation to the translations and a reference by Judge Rodrigues in the pre-trial Status Conferences, to the effect that exhibits could be tendered from the bar table when there is no dispute as to their authenticity, I would propose to tender those documents and the video at some stage during the week. Given that we do not have witnesses for Monday, other than Mr. Gavrankapetanovic, I wonder whether that may be a convenient time, if there is any legal argument from the Defence on that issue. Mr. President, as to how else we might use the time on Monday, I am in your hands in that regard. Every attempt has been made to bring forward other witnesses from next week to Monday, but so far unsuccessfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask the Defence whether there is any need to ask further questions to the expert witness Tabeau in respect of the newly presented answers to questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may be allowed. May I first respond to the questions raised by the Prosecution and then the question you yourself put, in that order, regardless of the time. Yes? We have lost a quarter of an hour listening to questions that could have been regulated out of court, and the Defence is not responsible for this. Secondly, regarding next week. You know that the Defence is working very late hours and it arises early to prepare the hearings, to study the documents, and it is absolutely impossible to extend working hours by an hour or two. Regarding the document we received today, we obviously haven't had time to discuss it. We will discuss it. But I do draw the attention of both the Prosecution and the Chamber to the fact that I take the plane this evening and I do not wish to make somebody come at my expense, as I have already done, and during the week, we will give you an answer but not before Monday. That would be impossible, before then. And finally, Mr. President, the last point, regarding page 14-15. I think that the Defence has always contested from the very beginning the GPS system, which means that we contested the system as a whole and therefore also the figures. Not just one or other figure. We have always challenged the admissibility of this system. And therefore, that made the position of the Defence be quite clear in the transcript. Global challenge of the GPS technology as such. And would you please remind me of the last question that you raised, because I seem to have forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was about expert witness Tabeau, whether there was any --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite. I apologise. I think we still haven't seen -- received the last from expert Tabeau. And when we are informed, we will be able to respond. Expert Tabeau should have brought some figures to complement her expert report, and I don't think that we saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you -- it's a three-page document that at least we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that we did receive them yesterday, but I personally did not see them. That is my mistake, and I apologise. But we will be able to provide an answer very soon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I -- I do understand that you -- it's difficult for you to respond to many requests, but I'd like to invite the Defence at least to see on the issue we dealt with closed session, but whether we could have a response on that, if possible, after the break. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Arrived at the moment where your next witness could be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I call Richard Higgs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: While he's coming, Mr. President, you indicated at an earlier time that you would have some preliminary questions for Mr. Higgs. Do you wish me to qualify him first or ask those questions beforehand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the issues we raised before is the factual basis of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Incident number one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Incident number one, was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The statements he -- or what are the sources of his factual knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's an important issue, especially if these are statements of witnesses that have not yet been in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's our first concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, whilst the witness is being brought in, in relation to that issue, by reference to the expert's report, I think the affected documents are on page 7 under the heading "Report on incident 1, June 1993," references B and C. In relation to page 8 of the report, under the heading "Report on incident 12 July 1993," Reference A, I think, is the subject of an appeal, and B -- in relation to B, we -- that's an issue which hasn't yet been resolved, whether (redacted) will give evidence next week or not. I propose to obtain the witness's opinion in such a way as to make clear what changes he would make to that opinion, if it wasn't for the material from sources A and B. I'll deal with the witness statements in respect of the first shelling incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I usually wish the witnesses a safe trip home again, but perhaps I should first wish them a safe trip to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We did -- we did check, Mr. President, before today's -- this afternoon's sitting to ensure he was in the witness room. So I don't know what's gone wrong. In the interest of saving time, some documents that I intend to show to the witness could perhaps be distributed, in particular MFI 5, 13, 14, and 15, which are the diagrams that were shown to Major Christian Bergeron have been photocopied and I have those available for the Defence and for Your Honours. Perhaps I could distribute those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that usually documents are distributed by the usher, who is at this moment not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Higgs, I presume. From your nodding, I take it that you do hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration. The text of this solemn declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher, and may I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Higgs. Please be seated. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your full name Richard James Higgs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 20th of October, 1959?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until two months ago, were you a member of the British army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you retire upon completion of 22 years of service?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that in fact a compulsory retirement requirement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness please be shown Exhibit number 3734.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document before you as being a report that you prepared and signed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please turn to page 7 of the report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the French booth is telling me that they haven't seen the report. So it would be useful that they be given a copy in the interest of the clarity of the French transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any extra copy available for the French booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution, in fact, provided copies of the report to the interpreters yesterday. If they don't have them today, it would seem that they haven't been passed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: From the interpreters yesterday. Perhaps that might be just checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I can give you one back.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We also have a spare copy at the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could even have some more languages then. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 7, do you see your subheading "Report on incident 1 June 1993"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I've just handed the usher another spare copy if the interpreters require it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that subheading?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then list three references, the last two being certain witness statements. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you, for the purposes of your opinion, to disregard anything that you read in those two witness statements. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I will take you now -- I will come back to that issue in a moment. But in the meantime, I take you over the page. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the page to the subheading "Report on incident 12 July 1993," followed by three references. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to disregard the sources listed as A and B. I will come back to that. Please now return to page 7. And I would ask you to focus on the material you are left with, having disregarded witness statements B and C, that is, items B and C under the subheading "References." Sir, did you inspect the certain crater impact sites in the car park?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sources, if any, did you use in order to identify the relevant crater impacts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I was shown the relevant crater impacts applicable to this particular incident. They were filled in with a set of material which identified them as the craters, and it was from that then I could determine my analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did, in addition to them being pointed out, did you have access to any written material which referred to the craters as being filled in with a red substance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that written material?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: There was a statement made by a member of the public who was present on the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I think if I remember right his name was Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not an objection. That is why I haven't said I object, Mr. President. I'm trying to take notes, as you know. And this is going very fast and I'm not succeeding. So could we ask you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we try to slow down also for the interpreters but also, since the Defence must be able to make its notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. Mr. President, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, evidence to the same effect as Mr. Fazlic's statement has been given, and I will now provide the references to that evidence according to the LiveNote transcript, that is, at pages 6620 at line 19, evidence to the effect that the relevant craters were filled in with a red substance; secondly at page 6622 at line 22, the witness Mr. Fazlic clarified that only those two crater impacts and no others were filled in with a red substance. That evidence was given on the 4th of April, 2002.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, having examined the crater impacts, did you take note of the shape of them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like the witness and the Trial Chamber to view two --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this question, it would be better to ask the witness what he did directly instead of leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what would be the best way to ask a question is a different thing than from whether it's admissible or not. I think the question about whether the witness took note of the shape is not leading to an extent which would make the question inadmissible. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like the witness now to view two scenes from video exhibit P3281B. For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, that was a video showing Mr. Fazlic pointing out certain features of the site relevant to shelling incident number 1. Perhaps the witness's video could be switched to the appropriate channel so he can view it as well. And once that is done, perhaps the video -- members of the video unit would display the first scene, which with the assistance of Mr. Sachdeva was lined up before the session began.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Stop, please. And perhaps that image could be maintained on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir do you recognise the image which appears on the screen at the moment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in particular, do you recognise the markings on the road in front of the gentleman with the walking stick?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: By the markings, I presume you mean the marks left by the crater?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do those markings indicate what you recollect to be the mortar impact site that was filled in with a red substance, at least one of them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I wonder if we can get a stiller image on the screen. Apparently we cannot. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us any features of significance in relation to the pattern of that mortar impact.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From the pattern of a mortar impact, it is possible to ascertain the approximate calibre of the weapon, and it's also possible to determine the angle or the approximate angle of descent. And thirdly, the direction from which the round came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What information were you able to glean from your inspection of this mortar impact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Although a long time had passed, obviously the crater is now not in as good a condition as it would have been originally. It is still possible to identify the direction from which the round came and still possible to approximate the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what direction did that mortar come from, that is, the mortar that created those markings on the parking lot surface?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The more accurate determination of that was done, of course, at the time by the investigating bodies. And when I inspected these craters, there was nothing I could see which would disagree with their findings. And their findings were approximately, if I can remember, 138 to 143 degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As one looks at the mortar impact markings on the screen at the moment, there appears to be more markings on one side than on the other. Does that accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. This is what we would normally expect to see on a mortar crater when a round hits the ground at a -- an average type of angle. So it's neither too shallow an angle or too steep an angle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a mortar shell impacts on contact, does the shrapnel leave the shell or, indeed, does the shell firstly become shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Could you clarify that question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the mortar shell impacts on contact, does the shell become part of the shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it leave its position as part of a shell in a way which radiates out from the line of the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That being the case, if it impact at an angle, do you expect to see shrapnel more on one side of the point of impact than on the other?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. If the -- the round hits the ground at an average type of angle, then there will be more distress on one side of the crater than the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having regard to your evidence and your report, is the side which has the greater distress the side closest to the launching point of the mortar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the mortar comes down at 90 degrees, that is, straight down, would you expect to see a symmetrical pattern having regard to that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The steeper the angle of descent, then you then expect to see a more cylindrical or even pattern.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, having regard to the image that was on the screen a few moments ago, there appears to be more distress closer to the video camera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Putting it simply, does that indicate that the source of fire of that mortar shell was in the direction in which the video camera person was standing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, I ask that the video now be fast-forwarded to the second relevant portion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please stop the video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the transcript, this second site -- at least, the relevant image also displays a Golf motor vehicle, or at least a Volkswagen motor vehicle with the number plate 582-J-593. Do you recognise the markings which appear on the surface of the carpark?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that accord with your recollection of the appearance of the other mortar impact site that you examined and which had been filled in with a red substance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What observations, if any, would you make about the direction of fire, having regard to the impact pattern?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This pattern was similar, if not very nearly the same, as the previous crater. You can see from the picture that, as we look at it, and there is more distress on the right-hand side than on the left, which would indicate that direction that the round came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- I have no further questions in relation to the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness's screen could be returned to the transcript mode.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist the -- yes. Oh, it's done from there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown some maps which have been tendered. They are Exhibit P3727. To assist Madam Registrar, they are the five shelling maps that were tendered through Mr. Karavelic. Whilst that is happening -- I'm grateful that they're ready to be shown to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, have you been shown copies of these maps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please turn to map number 1. I think it contains a box which reads "Shelling incident 1A-1B"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you also prepare a map yourself in relation to this incident and some of the other incidents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed all five shelling incidents that appear in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown Exhibit P3644.RH. Now, I'm not sure where the ELMO is in this courtroom, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there is an ELMO just to the left of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the relevant part of this map, that is, the right-hand part of Dobrinja, be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, it's the lower part of the map, approximately in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, we see a green line on the map. Did you plot the green line on the map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That can be seen on the screen at the moment in the south-eastern portion of Dobrinja. Did you plot the other green lines which appear in various positions on the map as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do they indicate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: On the information I was given, they indicate the confrontation lines at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I draw your attention to the part of Dobrinja that you inspected, in particular the site of the two crater impact points in the car park. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please take a -- I think it's a blue marker and place the number "1" alongside that impact point. Just a minute. Before you mark it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I give the court usher a pen with a finer point than the usual one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as long as it is blue, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, it seems, in relation to that incident, you have plotted in red two continuous lines and two broken lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what they represent and on what information you plotted those four lines.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The two solid lines represent the readings, were taken by the investigating team at the time, which I -- if I may just refer to the notes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Was 138 and 143 degrees. For crater analysis, we always have a factor of 5 degrees or approximately 100 mils, which we then draw on the outside of these lines basically to give us that degree of error. As crater analysis is not exactly precise, we always say that it is within plus or minus of 5 degrees, we have to show those lines on the outside of the readings that were taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you have with you in the -- at the witness's table a copy of the report of Captain B. Houdet in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you please take that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that document is contained in a bundle of documents which is have been filed with the Trial Chamber. They are identified as P3734A. And the translation is .1. And in that bundle towards the end, that report appears. It's titled "Crater analysis, Annex A."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that report now in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I will now take you through that report. The top line reads "Subject: Mortar attack at Dobrinja, June 1st at 10H20B." Do you know what that reference is, "10H20B"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does that translate into the 12-hour clock -- sorry, 24-hour clock?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: 10H, meaning 10 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The "20," meaning minutes. And the Bravo, meaning the zoning which the time was taken, which is Bravo times, which is 2 hours plus of Greenwich Mean Time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thereafter we see grid references. Do those references in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. particular refer to a series - a map being from a particular - on a particular scale?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, the grid -- the grid references show me the scale of map that was used and their location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Incidentally, perhaps this document should be placed on the ELMO, Mr. President, if we have a copy of it. I have a copy of the document so that the witness may keep his own copy in front of him. Perhaps the ELMO could be enlarged. That will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we move on to crater 1, which reads "Splinter pattern indicates mortar, minimum calibre 81 MM." Firstly, did the -- did your observations accord with that calibre, that is, your observations of the impact site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reading on: "Bearing to origin of fire: 140 degrees (2500 mils)." I think you mentioned earlier that you plotted the firm red lines at 143 degrees and 138 degrees; is that correct? Perhaps you could give that again, if I haven't stated it correctly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. The original ascertation of bearing decided from 138 to 143 degrees. I found nothing on my examination of the craters to disbelieve that information, and those two lines marked on the map are at 138 and 143 degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reading on: "Due to macadam, there is no fuse furrow." What is macadam?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Macadam is what we would call tarmac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is a fuse furrow?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: When a mortar bomb detonates, the fuse on certain types of ground is forced down into the ground and produces, for want of a better word, a hole. If we have this hole produced by the fuse, it can be then used to determine an accurate angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reading on -- recapping first: "There is no fuse furrow, so that angle of descent and range cannot be determined. Crater 2: Splinter pattern indicates mortar of same calibre." I stop there for a moment. Did you see anything which contradicted that conclusion as to the calibre of the second mortar impact site -- second mortar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reading on: "Bearing to origin of fire: 138 degrees (242 mils). Due to macadam, there is no fuse furrow, so that angle of descent and range cannot be determined." Next heading: "Conclusions." 1: The distance between crater 1 and the roof of the buildings indicates a minimum angle of descent of 40.5 degrees." I pause there. Is that consistent with your observations, having regard to the distance of the craters from the buildings to the east?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reading on: "2, under conclusions, the minimum angle of descent for 81 MM and 120 MM mortars is 45, 71 degrees." First of all, "45, 71," what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: These are the minimum angle descents for those particular weapon systems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean 45 degrees for an 81 millimetre and 71 degrees for a 120 millimetre, or does it mean 45 degrees in 71 minutes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From what has been written here -- the 81, it is definitely 45 degrees. But for 120s, some 120s have higher angles than others, and some would be 70 to 71 degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, does that -- I take it from the way you phrased that answer that that accords with your understanding of the minimum angles of descent of mortars. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the minimum angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Reading on: "At that angle, the minimum range is 1120 metres for 81 millimetre mortar, and 1340 metres or M, I should say, for 120 millimetre mortar." I pause. Does the "M" after the numbers indicate metres in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how do you interpret that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: What he has shown in that information is that if the mortars had fired on their minimum angles, then those are the ranges of which the round would possibly have gone or travelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll come back to that sentence in a moment. But reading on: Point 3, under conclusions: "Both bearings indicate that the shells can have been fired only from Serbian side. At the minimum range, the mortars were 300 M south of Lukavica barracks." Point 3 consists of two sentences that I've just read. Do you agree or disagree with the first of those sentences, that is, "both bearings indicate that the shells can have been fired only from Serbian side"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do the bearings assist in indicating that the shells could have only been fired from the Serbian side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: On the bearings that have been calculated, along that line in the direction of the confrontation line, the confrontation line is approximately only 270 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me just ask you to pause there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ierace, looking at the transcript. The question was: Do you agree or disagree? And the answer was, "Yes, I do." You have to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with that sentence or do you disagree with that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I agree with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your answer you indicated the distance from the points of impact to the confrontation line. How did you establish that distance? I think you said it was 275 metres -- 270 metres.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From the locations on the confrontation lines which I was given, I then measured from the mortar craters to that confrontation line along the line or the bearing that was calculated to come up with that distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that on a map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was it the map that you plotted -- the green line that you used for that exercise, or was it a different map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It was on a different map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was it on the first map that I showed you, that is, the coloured map which had marked on it "Shelling incident 1A and 1B," or a different map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It was on that map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And how did you obtain -- perhaps you could -- if that map is still on the table somewhere, if you could put that on the ELMO so that we can all see the relevant part. Could you please explain to us how you calculated the distance as being 270 metres.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: By taking a -- a ruler, placing it along the bearing lines, as I will just show on here. So placing the ruler between the points of impact and then measuring from there to the confrontation line. Then taking that distance and laying it across the grid intersection lines, which you can just see in this area here, you have the small graduations, which are 100 metres apart. Lay it across there, and then read off the distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, given that the distance between the grids is one kilometre, does that mean that in order to obtain an approximate measurement, regardless of the extent to which a map is enlarged or reduced, one can always refer the distance between two points on the map to the grid in order to determine that approximate distance? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. Those graduations are 100 metres apart, so you can always use those to calculate the distance between two points. And if your point falls between two of those graduations, then you then interpolate between the two points to try and give you a more accurate distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on this map we see that the boxes are not entirely square; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand this to be an electronic map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you please now go to the map that you plotted and look at these -- the grid references on that map. And having regard to the image of that map on the screen, is it the position that the grids are square -- are true squares, or so it appears? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In other words, is it easier to plot distances which -- between points which run at an angle, that is, not north-south or east-west on a map such as the one on the screen at the moment which has square grids?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is more accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I note the time, Mr. President. Perhaps over the break the witness could look at the distances on the square map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have a ruler? Do you have a ruler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever the witness does something or looks at something during the break, there should be someone present so in order to make sure that he does not consult anyone. Unfortunately the legal officer is not there to replace. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'd like to just avail myself of this opportunity in order for the Prosecution not to waste time. Since he was asked not to consider letters B, C of the aforementioned incident, could we now please erase all the conclusions from his report, anything that he would have drawn from B, C, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This would be, I would say, a question. Either you make an objection or by suggesting that the conclusions are not right, that's of course a different thing. So either you do that in cross-examination or you object in another way. But suggestions as to whether we could strike all the conclusions are not the way of making objections. It's more a question, a suggestion. It's not quite clear to me. But I feel that the Defence thinks that that should be the consequence of what the witness -- the expert witness said. Is that -- am I correctly understanding you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I will come back to that. Just this witness was asked not to pay attention to B, C of the sources; therefore, there must be something in his report that has to be taken out, and I would like to propose for that to be taken out during the break. But I withdraw my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the suggestion is withdrawn, it needs no further attention. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to save time, might I instruct the witness to make the same calculations in relation to the other four incidents of the map with the square grids. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so. We'll adjourn until twenty minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give the opportunity to the Prosecution to resume the examination of the witness, may I ask whether the Defence could tell the Chamber in such a way that we don't have to go into closed session whether there's an objection against the measures sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking us, Mr. President, with respect to the documents dated the 26th, or are we speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- you have it in front of you. It's page 5997 up till 6003. That's the issue we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are any objections we have to turn to closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be an objection, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we perhaps use this last few minutes before the next break to see whether we have to turn into closed session. Yes. Then please, Mr. Ierace, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, have you done those calculations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In relation to shelling incident number 1, what was the distance between the impact sites and the confrontation line approximately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Along the -- the direction line, the distance comes out approximately at 320 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incident number 2?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: 250 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 3?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 4?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: 450 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 5?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: 2320 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in relation to incident number 1, I take you back to the report -- I withdraw that. In relation to incident number 1, you've told us that when a mortar descends at 90 degrees or thereabouts, you expect to see a symmetrical impact pattern; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. The steeper the angle of descent towards 90 degrees, the more symmetrical the pattern becomes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In theory, how close to an impact site can a mortar be fired? In theory.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Mortars are capable of firing to very close ranges. It is possible for a mortar to put a round down probably within 50 metres of its own location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that was to happen, in what direction or at what angle, I should say, would the mortar tube be? Relation to the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: To achieve a minimum range of that dimension, the mortar barrel would be at maximum elevation for that particular model of mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, would it be pointing almost straight up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the trajectory of a mortar shell, what shape is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The trajectory, if a mortar, for example, is fired at approximately at 45 degrees, you would expect the descent angle to be slightly greater. It is not a perfect curve. The mortar bombs tend to fall at a slightly steeper angle to the angle they were fired at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that something which is taken into account when analysing a mortar crater impact pattern?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, mortars can be fired with different charges or different numbers of charges according to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere, Mr. Ierace. Could you explain how you could take this into account, or were you going to ask questions about that? Could you tell us -- the question was whether the slightly steeper angle on which the shell descends is taken into account when analysing the impact pattern. Could you explain how you take that into account. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The angles that we use are produced in what are called firing tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And those firing tables dictate or tell you the different angles. And from those tables, you can then work out the ranges that that weapon would have been fired at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, you would say is that the slightly flatter angle of firing would be taken into account when calculating, on the basis of your observation of the angle of descent, the range.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it has got nothing to do with the interpretation of the pattern itself. So the pattern is used to establish the angle of descent. And then for your further calculations, you use the slight difference in angles of descent compared to the angle of firing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The pattern itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Is never used solely to determine an angle of descent. It is only a guide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- To calculate angle of descent accurately, you need a fuse furrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Failing a fuse furrow, then you can use tail fins for approximate angle of descent, if present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the pattern will show you is whether it's come in at a very low descent angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An average descent angle somewhere in the centre or a very steep descent angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's a very global estimate of what the angle would have been.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that still does not explain how you use the difference in angle of descent compared to the angle of firing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The angle of descent is specified in range tables. It is calculated by different ordnance boards or ballisticians. Not by us. We use their figures that they give us, which then show angles of descent in relation to angles of firing. It is not a calculation that we conduct ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's not a matter of analysis of the pattern. But once you have established a global angle of descent, then by using tables or someone else using tables, you establish what would be then the approximate angle of firing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand you. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take you now back to the [redacted] [redacted]. Do you have that nearby?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there's a problem with the French booth. They tell me they don't have this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have a spare copy, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay. I have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you or could --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That should be Captain Houdet, [redacted] I think that probably explains the lack of report. I see shaking of heads. That doesn't explain it. Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is an annex to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The report I wish the witness to refer to is Houdet, H-O-U-D-E-T. Mr. President, might there [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Do you have a number, Mr. Ierace, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is contained within Exhibit ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's the document that the witness had earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I take you back to the conclusions, in particular conclusion 2, second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The confusion might be, Mr. Ierace, is that the crater analysis is both an annex to Exhibit P3743A, and it seems to be a single page that the witness had. I remember you asked him whether he had present -- that, of course, could create some confusion. Perhaps you instruct him clearly which copy or which -- which of these documents to use. Perhaps the best way of doing it, Mr. Ierace, is that this crater analysis is already admitted into evidence as Exhibit P1367. Perhaps we should present that to the witness so that there's no further confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That would be convenient, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before I take you to that, Mr. Higgs, in order for a mortar to be fired at the minimum possible distance, would you expect it to have one charge or more than one charge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: To obtain the minimum distance, you require the mortar to be fired on its minimum charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Earlier you said that the appearance of the mortar craters was consistent with the report of Captain Houdet to the effect that the craters were created by mortars of a calibre of 81 millimetres. What is the minimum -- what is the maximum distance that you would expect an 81-millimetre mortar shell to travel on one charge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Different manufacturers of medium mortars of 81- or 82-millimetre calibre, depending on the type of ammunition, will give you different ranges. Older ammunitions may have a maximum range of approximately two to three thousand metres. Newer and more modern ammunition can give you ranges from five to seven thousand metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the minimum range you would expect from one charge of an 81-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The minimum range is normally governed by the weapon type rather than ammunition, and with most mortars it's a figure of about 50 to 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this case, you've told us that having regard to the report and to your own observations, the angle of descent of the mortar was, I think you said, within an average range or a normal angle; is that correct? Perhaps you could expand on that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The overall shape of the crater basically shows me that the angle of descent was not one fired at an extremely low angle of descent, and it was not one of extremely high angle of descent, as the pattern doesn't show that. The shape is what you would expect to see if the round came in at what we would call a normal angle, probably somewhere between 50, 55 degrees and 70 degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What conclusions, if any, can you draw as to the distance from which the mortars were fired, having regard to that range of angles of descent for an 81 -- for 81-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Using that angle of descent, even if fired on a low charge, the range of the mortar would be somewhere from five or six hundred metres upwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the mortars had been fired from within, say, 320 metres, what would you expect the level of the volume of sound to have been as heard from the sites of impact; that is, the sound of the mortars being fired?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: A firing position within 320 metres, the noise level would be quite high, and you would expect even around that location where there were buildings, of course for people to hear that sound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you expect maybe one or two people with sensitive hearing to hear it, or would you expect people generally to hear it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I would expect people generally to hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might the witness be shown MFI -- MFIs 13, 14, and 15. In particular, MFI 15. I think that is the diagram which shows three parabolic curves marked A, B, and C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, you've told us earlier that -- I withdraw that. Would you assume for the sake of this exercise that the curves on the sheet of paper in front of you are trajectories of mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And perhaps the diagram could be placed on the ELMO, so that we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that such trajectories are not symmetrical, in other words, that the descent is more steeper than the ascent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Correct. The descent is always steeper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've also given us a range of angles of descent for these two particular mortars. And having regard to the curves in front of you, do any of the curves, that is, A, B, or C, approximate in terms of the angle of descent that range that you earlier indicated? Do they come within that range, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Out of those three curves, the one nearest to the craters in question would be the curve on the screen which is B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming back to the report of Captain Houdet -- do you still have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, is there anything in conclusions 2 or 3 that you would disagree with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In conclusion 2, Captain Houdet has made the point of telling us the minimum range if fired at the minimum angle. What he has not done is determine the range from the possible angle of descent in this case, because a mortar very rarely fires on its minimum angle, and so therefore you would get, obviously, a shorter range if it was fired at an angle greater than 45 degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If I could just come back to my question: Is there anything in those four sentences, that is, the sentences in conclusions 2 or 3 that you would disagree with? I appreciate that you have added something that you would expect to be in the report. But is there anything there that you -- with which you do not concur?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The final statement where it says the mortars were 300 metres south of the barracks, I think that statement is difficult to prove because with the angle of descent, he has calculated that of 45 degrees, which I believe to be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, some of those materials might now be returned, P1367, which is the report of Captain Houdet. And perhaps the maps could stay with the witness for the time being; the MFIs 13, 14, and 15 could also be returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to shelling incident number 2, you have placed some markings on the map, being red unbroken lines and red broken lines. Were they -- do they represent the same type of feature as in shelling incident number 1?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What was your source of information in order to plot those lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: My source of information was the forensic report that was carried out at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having regard to page 8 of your report, do you mean reference number A?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you had to disregard the forensic report, would you nevertheless be able to determine the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Without that information --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are asking this witness to do something impossible. He says, "My source of information was such and such," and then we're -- then he's being asked what his source of information was. So the way the question has been put leads to an impossible answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that the first question was what his source was, and the second question is whether he could have come to the same conclusions when he would not have used those sources but only other sources. I think that's, as such, not an impossible question. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The findings that I found in that particular reference were also backed up by those in reference B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And if you had to regard both references A and B, would you be left with any information which would enable you to determine the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: At this time the -- obviously the location and there was no evidence left at this time, so therefore my findings were taken from those two references. Without those two references, it would be very difficult, if not nearly impossible, to ascertain the direction of fire at this period in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, coming back to your opinion based on references A and B and C, you refer in your report -- I withdraw that. When you visited that site, did you observe a place which you understood to have been utilised in relation to a tunnel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I was shown that location, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that location on the map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I can identify that location on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you firstly with the thin blue pen place a "2" alongside the impact point of the mortar in the same way as you placed a "1" alongside the impact points for 1.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
