utterances.text: And will you now, please, place a small cross at the point which you understood to be the -- well, firstly, how was the point described to you when you visited it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I was shown the point on the ground by one of the members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you understand it to be -- to be what, the beginning of a tunnel or the entrance to a tunnel or a waiting point for a tunnel or what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: As an entrance to a tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Will you please place a cross with the blue pen to indicate the point or the place that was pointed out to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Alongside that, would you place the capital letter "T."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you, when you visited the site, measure the distance between that point and the point of mortar impact for incident 2?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: On the day I measured the distance as it was in a straight line, straight down the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that distance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Approximately 120 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have plotted on this map the direction of fire with a firm red line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the tunnel entrance along that line of fire or direction of fire if you extended it, or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No, it isn't. The tunnel entrance is, from the direction of fire, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. off to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What observations, if any, would you make on the theory that the intended target was not the water line, but the area immediately in front of the tunnel entrance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Now, the evidence, as I have it, does not lead to that -- for me to make that conclusion, as the round has missed by quite a considerable distance, take into account that this is a city location and some of the factors that go with that. And also, that -- then the tunnel was not reengaged with a more accurate round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the difference in angle? Is that of any significance or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The degree by which it has missed would not be one I would expect to see if this target had been pre-recorded. It is too great. And for that reason, it makes me believe that the round did hit its intended target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, more generally in relation to pre-recorded targets. Assuming that for the sake of this question -- I notice Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to ask the counsel to slow down, please, and the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, if you look at the screen, as soon as the text stops moving, if you then answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, I want to know whether mortars over a period of time are capable of hitting pre-recorded targets accurately. And I'd like you to factor in for your answer that the mortars are kept in the same position, that is, with the base plates in the same position, over a period of weeks and months, even years, and that the crews are constant -- in other words, those operating the mortars are the same individuals over such periods of time. To what extent could a mortar crew, in those circumstances, hit a target which they had previously hit and recorded, say, weeks beforehand?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Basically, yes, they would be capable of hitting this target, but there are certain factors that you need to be aware of. Normally the main errors with mortar firing would be that of human error and weather conditions. In a city-type location, map-reading is made easier for one reason -- for one point. And if mortars were in position for such a long time, their base plates would be solid in the ground, i.e. There'd be no movement, they would have time to have corded charges, bearings, elevations to all these points. The only factor that is left which could give problems is the weather. But this can easily be taken into account with either firing the mortars sometime in that particular day, earlier on, or the day before in similar weather conditions, or, of course, having, if available, a computer that analyses data for you. So because the mortars were in position for so long, taking all those points into account, it is safe to say that you would expect the accuracy of the mortars to be greatly enhanced and you would not expect them to miss by hundreds of metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the weather can be taken into account," for instance, in relation to wind speed, are there calculations available which allow mortar crews to mathematically make an approximate adjustment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: If you do not have the -- the computers that do it for you, then again by using range tables, in those tables there are allowances for wind, by knot speed. So if you know the wind direction and its speed, you can add those calculations into your information for the mortar before firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even without such tables, where you have the same crews operating from the same mortars, firing to the same targets, would you expect them to develop a degree of expertise in terms of adjusting their mortars to take into account variations of temperature, wind, and humidity?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is hypothetical and leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For an expert witness hypothetical questions are not excluded. And as far as whether it's leading, I would first like to give an opportunity to Mr. Ierace to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I am seeking from this expert an expert opinion. And in order to do that, I have to give him certain variables to factor in. In order to give him the variables, a question has to be in a leading form, but it must not suggest the answer, and the question does not suggest the answer. It simply gives him specific variables to factor into his response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied. Please proceed. Perhaps you could repeat the question, Mr. Ierace, or ask the witness to read it from the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your question is correct. With the same people operating for such a long period of time, it would be safe to assume that they will have local knowledge of how much those variables affected where they were firing and therefore would be able to take them into account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I now move to incident number 3. Would you place the number "3" with the thin blue pen alongside the relevant impact points.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your report, you said that you visited the site.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you noted that mortars of two different calibres were used.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that if they "were fired as one mission" - and I am now quoting from your report at page 9 -"then it appears to have a deliberate attempt to kill the civilians in that area by making them run for cover and then targeting the routes. If this is so then it would be a deliberate-type ambush." I think they are the words that appear in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that were so, do the crater -- do the mortar impact sites, having regard to the evidence of the children and adults killed, do they indicate to you any degree of precision? In other words, what degree of precision does that information and your observations indicate on the part of the crews responsible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The two craters in question landed in front of the buildings at varying distances from the buildings but on routes of access to those buildings. The two rounds -- the distance between them was greater than what I would expect to see if it was just what we call the zone of a mortar, i.e., the -- the accuracy of the mortar or the -- the natural spread, if you like. The distance between them would actually show either pre-recording of that point or a deliberate adjustment between those two points so as to fire one and then move the barrel before firing the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that things are going -- moving far too fast. I did not want to interrupt the witness, but I'm doing it now because I must do it. It is in relation to the correct quote by the Prosecution of a sentence by witness, including the term "deliberate." The witness is, perhaps, an expert in weapons, but he cannot speak about the intent, that is, about the deliberate character of an action. So in this sense, the objection is that even if he has written this, I don't think that he can be asked questions about a deliberate character of something. This does not include -- is not included in his technical expertise, but this is something that your Chamber is to decide on. Thank you -- if this is the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to re-read the question, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question makes more sense against the background of the answer before it. Unfortunately we don't have LiveNote here today, so I can't scroll up, because we have different computers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In fact, I could do that, because I asked my LiveNote to be restored. So I will -- although it's quite confusing because now I have other pages, since it has been installed only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm happy to rephrase the question, Mr. President, to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you could do that, although I found it meanwhile. Mr. Ierace, I think Mr. Piletta-Zanin is right that interpreting what was in the mind of those who were firing is, I would say, not within the expertise. On the other hand, which would be according to the experience of a -- of an expert witness, would be rational behaviour or could be explained in a rational way is a different matter. So we are touching an area where we have to be very careful. I would agree with that. And if you reformulate your question, we'll hear whether we -- whether our concern is taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, having regard to your report, you note that investigations at the time established that a mortar shell of calibre 120 millimetres fell behind the building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thereafter, two 82-millimetre calibre shells fell on the street side of the relevant buildings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were given a witness statement which is reference C in your report; is that so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that witness statement make clear that as the first shell fell, immediately following on the first shell falling the children who were playing in the street ran to the entrances to the buildings? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you understand the evidence to be that as they did that, two shells in quick succession landed near two separate entrances to the buildings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. One round landed, and then followed shortly after with the second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, assuming, for the sake of the question that that evidence is correct, does that indicate anything to you in terms of the precision that the responsible mortar crews were capable of?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. It is a leading question, and it's implicating the fact -- or it's inferring that the -- those who targeted, those who fired were able to see, although we don't even know whether they were able to see the target. And what's being ruled out is the hypothesis that the firing -- they could have just landed randomly. So, this is a leading question. When I say -- I don't mean randomly. I meant by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would have thought it was obvious from earlier evidence, but I'm happy to clarify it for my friend by asking a preliminary question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, when a mortar crew operates, does it normally rely on observers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. But it is possible to fire without them on recorded targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When -- in other words, when you refer to recorded targets, do you mean where they are ordered to hit a target which has previously been recorded and fired upon?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the normal operation of a mortar crew involve a forward observer, in radio contact with the mortar crew commander directing, fire, that is, either confirming the target has been hit or giving instructions on what adjustment needs to be made to the fire, in terms of distance and direction?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I press the question, Mr. President, against the background of that response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained, Mr. Ierace. Whether a mortar crew is capable of precision firing while hitting certain targets, I think it would go beyond the expertise of the expert witness to give an answer to that question. If you would have asked him whether a capable mortar crew might have succeeded in hitting two entrances of a building, that's a different thing. But if you hit two entrances of a building and you intended to hit the entrances of two other buildings, then hitting these entrances would say nothing about capability, so therefore this is not a question which could be answered within the expertise of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand the reasoning, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, if the intended targets for the two shells that landed on the street were in fact the areas where they landed, does that indicate anything to you as to whether the tubes had been placed in a position where they had fired in that direction or area previously? In other words, if they landed where they were supposed to, having regard to your earlier evidence as to the degree of accuracy that can be achieved by base plates being in the same position day after day, week after week, month after month, does this give any such indication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object because, first of all, we don't know whether base plates, whether they were fixed, whether they were stable. And also, again this is a very hypothetical question in a sense that, in any case, if firing hits a target, this could be by mistake, because it was pre-prepared, so everything is open, so it doesn't lead to much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question misunderstands -- the response rather by my learned colleague misunderstands the question. The question assumes that the intended targets were hit and works backwards from that. Given, hypothetically, that the intended targets were hit on the first shots, what conclusions, if any, can one draw as to the permanency or otherwise of the positions of the mortars? And that draws directly on the earlier evidence of the witness as to the degree of accuracy which mortars are capable on a first shot where the base plate has not been moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just reading and trying to better understand both the objection and your response, Mr. Ierace. Yes. May I ask you one question before, perhaps, conferring with my colleagues. What probative value would the answer of such a question have? I mean, it -- it says more or less that if you are hitting the target you intended to hit, would that mean that everything should be stable in order to make it possible for you to hit such a target?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Probative value goes beyond that. The probative value of the question is whether the mortars that fired the shells had been effectively pointed in that direction for an extended period of time. The relevance of that, in turn, is to certain propositions which have been advanced by the Defence as to the source of fire where civilians on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. government side of the confrontation line were targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But still, on the basis of the assumption that the impact was on the target, which is, may say, uncertain. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. The Chamber sees no probative value in any possible answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As you please, Mr. President. Would you excuse me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, when typically a mortar crew fires to hit its target, fires with a particular target in mind, if the target is not hit on the first round, having regard to your earlier evidence as to the use of observers, what expectation, if any, can one have as to the -- the positions that the subsequent mortar shells land in? Would you expect them to be closer to the target or further from the intended target, or the same distance from the intended target?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object. This is an objection because we have seen a lot of things in terms of technical side of firing. There are self-firing, which is very rapid. A crew person would fire, and then the rounds would still be up in the air and they would be fired again before the first shell lands. So if this was a salvo fire, then the shell will follow the first trajectory of the previous shells. So Mr. Ierace should perhaps take this into consideration and rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the question was clear enough. And if the witness has a problem with it, perhaps he could indicate it. It builds on evidence given five minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the objection is denied. Yes, the question is admissible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With typical mortar firing, if the observer observes his first round has missed the target, he will send the correction to those mortars to enable, of course, the second round to hit the target and thereby achieve his aim. He would have no point in firing mortar rounds in an area that he's missing the target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this incident, you indicate in your report that you read a shelling report by Mr. Verdy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any difference in the conclusions arrived at by him compared to the other report, that is the report by Roy Thomas -- sorry, the report referred to as reference A by Mr. Sabljica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The main differences is that Verdy did his investigation at a later point in time, which is never ideal. He also confused the calibre of the weapon that might have been used, again because the evidence of the 82 at that time would not have been there, as the forensic team was, obviously, already done that investigation. But his general bearing of which the mortars came from does back up the forensic report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the calibre of the mortars, when you inspected the craters on the street side, were you able to form any view as to approximately what calibre the mortars which created those impacts had been?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Although these craters are not well preserved due to the time, they are not of the size and destructive pattern that I would have expected to see if they were 120 millimetre as opposed to a medium mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Will you now, please, go on a map to the plottings that you made in respect of incident 4 and place the number "4" alongside the relevant impact points.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to that incident, you referred to -- you referred to a technical examination report. That's reference A. Did you read a report or reports made by Mr. Verdy --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I withdraw that. In relation to this incident, did you read the report by Mr. Sabljica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you also seen a report by Mr. Verdy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what comment, if any, would you make about any differences between those two reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The Verdy report, again, taken after the fact, although it differs very slightly from the forensic report, the differences are consistent with the sort of error I would expect to see anywhere on crater examination, and the Verdy report is nearly identical to that of the forensic report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you please now turn to incident 5 on the map and place the number "5" alongside the mortar impact point, as indicated?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might the witness be shown Exhibit 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: D61, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps now the usher could show the witness Exhibit D61.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you have looked at that, Mr. Higgs, may it be placed on the ELMO. Mr. Higgs, assuming that the items which appear in the photograph D61 come from the one object originally, are you able to discern what type of shell that might have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President, objection, since we asked to obtain these objects in order to be able to verify whether they come from the same source. You know that those objects were mysteriously lost or they didn't want to give them to us, and we cannot ask questions supposing that, as the Defence was not allowed to question on these objects having them in physical existence, in their hands, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having regard to the document in front of you, do you recognise any of those objects?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you point -- first of all, do you recognise more than one piece or just one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: More than one piece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you point to one of the pieces that you recognise and hold the pointer on it while you tell us what you recognise it to be.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you pointing to a piece which is approximately U-shaped and slightly lighter in colour in shades of grey than the surrounding pieces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This piece here is the shape that I would expect to see of the fuse adapter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fuse adapter of what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The fuse adapter of a mortar round, calibre which, of course, I cannot determine from the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please point to another piece that you recognise.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You point to a piece almost in the top left of the photograph. What is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This piece is also part of a fuse adapter, again of a mortar round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise any other pieces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the one you are pointing to now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That particular part is consistent with a part of a fuse for a mortar round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any other pieces that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Those are the three main pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a photocopy of that exhibit. I ask that it be shown to the witness and he mark on it with numbers 1, 2, and 3 the pieces that he recognised and in the order in which he pointed them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. Mr. Usher, could you assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could that first be shown on the ELMO so that everyone can see it. Yes. I take it -- one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I move on, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you need a further look at it, you could have it. But please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, in your experience, do mortar tail fins ever end up in the crater created by the mortar exploding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever observed a tail fin to be embedded in a crater in hard ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in what circumstances you have made that observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stopped our expert just in time not to write anything on this piece of paper. My left hand is almost as quick as my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the excuses of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no -- nothing against again look at it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. But of course, adding anything to it won't be allowed. We do understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We cannot assume that technical experts won't always know what the practice is in the court. So there's no blame expressed. But happily you could prevent the expert from adding something of his expertise to the -- to the drawings. It would be time for a break, Mr. Ierace, if this would be a suitable moment. If not, tell us how much minutes you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: This would be a convenient time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then before we go into the break seek an answer, if necessary in closed session, on the question I put at the beginning of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the break or now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to have a response now. If you'd say there is an objection, we have to go into closed session in order to -- or at least private session. I think that would do for the moment. May I then ask, Mr. Usher, that you escort the expert witness out of the courtroom, and may I also ask the -- your expert to leave the courtroom already before giving an answer. Yes. Please -- both. May I ask you the escort the expert witness, Mr. Higgs, out of the courtroom. And may I at the same time ask the expert assisting the Defence to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to wait for one second. Yes. Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The other issue I would like to convey to the parties is that the Chamber has decided that it will seek an opportunity to sit for longer hours next week. Perhaps that's not possible in -- on each and every day. For example, Friday will not be possible as far as I understand. Perhaps one other day not as well. So we'll have to work out a schedule and we'll also have to see whether there are any claims by other cases. So we first have to deal with the matter with those in charge of the court calendar. But as a starting point, the Chamber is willing to find a couple of more hours. Of course within certain limits. But we'll try to find more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I express my gratitude to the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May then the witness be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very quickly while the usher is fetching the witness. It will take one minute for us to raise a technical issue at the end of the hearing. We will see whether we can organise ourselves better for Monday, but I am afraid that it will be very difficult, but I hope we will -- but I wish to say that we will find a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Higgs, I asked you whether, in your experience, tail fins had embedded in mortar craters where the ground was hard, and you said yes. And I asked you what the circumstances in your experience were. Perhaps I could ask you in what part of the world did you particularly notice this phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: There are two cases that immediately come to mind: Firstly, in Kenya, where the ground is extremely hard. Tail fins locate into the craters. And also one case I investigated in Germany, where a tarmac road crosses the middle of the impact area. We had a crater there again with tail fins still in the crater.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you refer to Kenya, was that your personal experience or what you heard from others? Were you in Kenya at some stage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: They were my personal experiences, as I was the senior safety officer for Kenya at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, earlier I asked you some questions about the ability or otherwise of mortar crews to repeatedly successfully hit pre-registered targets over a space of weeks. Where a mortar crew has a pre-registered target, does that assist them or not to target other places near the pre-registered target? In other words, does the pre-registered target assist or not in locating other specific targets which are not pre-registered?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. A mortar observer will always try and adjust a new target, where possible, going from a pre-recorded target, because that pre-recorded target has already had some of the errors shot out when that was recorded itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in terms of an urban battlefield, as was the case with the city of Sarajevo, what use, if any, could a mortar crew make of street maps and other detailed maps in terms of adjusting their tubes with the intention of hitting a specific building or intersection or other place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In a city environment, the reference points which you have in map reading are greatly increased. One of the human errors for inaccuracy with mortars is always map reading, identifying targetry. For instance, in a city where you have clear reference points on the ground which are then marked on a map, it makes the map reading far more accurate and reduces errors in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what is the minimum angle of descent of a mortar of 120 calibre?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: These vary depending on the manufacturer of the mortar, but they tend to be slightly greater than that of a medium mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some range of minimum angles of descent for 120-millimetre mortar; in other words, making allowances for different manufacturers.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: These would probably vary between approximately 50, up to 70 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That completes the examination-in-chief, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Higgs?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I just take 30 seconds to tidy up my papers on the desk, I will proceed, Mr. President. In the meantime, I would like to say good afternoon to the witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that you are an officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I have just recently retired, but my rank was quartermaster sergeant instructor, which is a rank of warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Sir, in order to save time, which is much more precious for the Prosecution than for the Defence now, I would ask you to answer clearly to my questions. Very well. When did you gain this rank?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I have been a warrant officer since 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, you went to Sarajevo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You perhaps had other contacts with -- perhaps you had some other contacts with the local circumstances; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As translated into the witness's language, the question reads: "You perhaps had other contacts with the local circumstances." Perhaps the question could be clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had contacts with local life, reality?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I maintain my objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know -- I don't know how it's translated into English, because I immediately changed to the French channel. Yes, the question is too vague. [Previous translation continues] ... If you go somewhere that you have contact with the that place, of the life of that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... If so many people have difficulties in understanding what a question is about and the Chamber would like to understand it as well, please reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, by contact with local reality, what I mean is you didn't just go into the city of Sarajevo but you were also led somewhere else, perhaps in the adjoining hills; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: While I was there, I was taken around the city and also around the local area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, did you decide by yourself to go to such and such a place, or were you in some way led to a certain place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Some of the locations I was taken to to show me certain things, but on some of the locations I requested to go and see parts in the local area for my own peace of mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm talking about locations around Sarajevo, and these locations which are not in the city but outside of the city. Did you ask to see certain locations, or were you taken there -- or were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Both of those happened. I was taken to some, and I requested to go to some others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the locations that you asked to see?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: One of the locations I asked to see was in respect with incident 5, the market incident, where I wanted to see possible locations where a mortar could be fired from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I will have to interrupt you. What I meant was outside of the city. That's what I asked.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This location is outside of the city. It's in the hills, to the north of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. Please proceed. You were taken to a location where the mortar had been fired from; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This obviously could not be confirmed. We don't know exactly where the mortar fired from. I wanted to see the ground where the roads, woods may be so I could either confirm areas or eliminate certain areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of Mr. Usher, could we please have a look again at the document. I believe that you have it. That is, document 4010. That is, P3727. These are the maps that you have in front of you. The very last page, which is in relation to incident number 5, please. And perhaps place it on the ELMO, please. Thank you. Thank you. That is for the booths. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you perhaps indicate on this map where supposedly -- where you were told that supposedly a mortar had been fired from. Supposedly, for the Serb booth -- Serbian booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has not given that evidence. The witness has said that he asked to be taken to some areas; in other words, that he was doing the directing. So perhaps it first should be clarified whether in fact the witness was told of certain places where -- I assume my friend means the mortar had been fired from. From the question, as translated, says "a mortar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the second question already, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you really distort the evidence of the witness up till that moment. So, if you have -- if you seek any confirmation of the witness, would you please not distort the testimony up to that moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to this incident, where were you taken, please, outside of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Working on the -- working on the information we had from the reports of the line of fire, we drove into the hills and looked at various areas really from approximately here and then up here and all around this particular area just to see if that type of area was capable of supporting mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And sir, could you please indicate at the same time below the green line and also above the line, still in relation to the red trajectories, red lines. And the site that you spoke about first, which is below the green line, could you tell its -- do you know its name? Could you tell it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, it would be appropriate for the witness to mark on the map the area he has indicated so as to record for the transcript what we have just seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to ask the same, but I think that in the next question it was incorporated, that the witness had pointed to places below and above the green line but always within the boundaries of the -- of the red lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As you please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. There is a problem of translation, since what I said was "since you have indicated this area below and above." That is clear for the transcript. The witness indicated one area below and one above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is the name of the area below, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I cannot see the names on the map. The locations I went to, I can identify on a quality map, but the names I -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, since you mentioned in your report some names above the line, why didn't you mention certain names below the line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In the area I went to, that part above Sarajevo, it is a -- a hilly terrain or mountainous terrain. From the locations where I went and working on the principle for mortar locations, you would not wish to site a mortar location on a forward slope. So, normally it would be on a rearward slope, out of sight of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No I have to interrupt you, sir. My question was: Why didn't you mention the name of the areas that you visited above this line, since you mention the names in relation to the area --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you visited the areas below this line, mention the names in the area above the line, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And not the names below the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The question posed by my friend assumes that his last answer was not responsive. In fact, if one looks at the reference in the report, the answer was responsive. And I appreciate that Your Honours have the report. I refer to page 12, first line. And on that basis, I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I think the question is why the witness did mention in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Locations that were below -- were above the green line and did not mention any of the spots he visited below the green line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And my point is that one first has to look at the context in which he mentioned the places above the line, which is the -- the context is, there being suitable sites to place a mortar. When one then considers the witness's answer, that is what he was saying, he didn't see suitable sites. So my question's friend -- I'm sorry, my --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to interrupt. What Mr. Ierace has just done constitutes the answer to my following question. If Defence had done this, this would have been dealt with differently in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've been interrupted. And with respect to my learned colleague, what I'm saying is directly relevant to the question to which I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed. I'll give you the reasons at the very end of this session. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to answer clearly why was it that you did not mention the name of the locations that you said that you allegedly visited below the green line.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The reason for this is, in my opinion, that would be an unlikely position for the mortars to be positioned, and therefore did not put them into the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you mention that you visited such areas, such locations, and that later on you could have said that you visited those areas and that you felt that they could not -- they were unlikely to be used as firing positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I have visited many, many areas around Sarajevo, and I have not listed them all in my reports. I've only listed the ones that I feel are relative or applicable to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you knew that in relation with this incident that some of the reports believed that the two areas, that is, the area below and the area above, that they were both possible areas from which the fire could have originated.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I have seen no reports that say anything from below the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me too? For the French booth. I can hear it as well. What is the problem? I believe that that is because I have the Serbian booth. But I can do this without the headphones. Is this better? Very well. Thank you. Is this better for the French booth? Thank you very much. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, I'm going to re-ask my question. Sir, did you know - yes or no - that there were other reports which said that the locations where the fire originated from could have been to the north or to the south of the green line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No. The only reports I have seen are the forensic and the other ones which I have reference to in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, when you allegedly visited the area, the area north of Sarajevo, south of the demarcation line, did you find still at the time the roads that the army that had occupied this area had built there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I was shown one of those such roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This was a road which allowed mechanical equipment to arrive there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I've got no idea of what they used the road for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm not talking about that, their use. I'm talking about their ability, their capability. Were these roads which were -- which allowed to the area for mechanised units; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I would presume they would be used for that purpose, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness,. Did you know, that is, were you told, that the army, the so-called BH Army, occupied or had under its control this area which you mentioned, south of the green line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the areas as marked by the green line on the map. So I was told that opposing forces were either side of this line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, near -- in the environs near this green line on this map, were you able to establish yourself the presence of rocky area, of rocky terrain, or of elevations, of high ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. There is a -- a high feature that runs along that point. Some of it is steeper than others and some of it, yes, is quite rocky.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are there more of these rocky features in this area or of elevations, of high ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you go to the top of these rocky features?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Not all of them. Just some.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On some of the rocky features that you did go to -- so we are still talking about the area below the green line. We agree on that; yes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The high features I visited, most of them were either on or above the green line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems that we do not have any interpretation in Serbian. In any case, that's what I'm being told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the problem solved now? Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I also ask you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to find a suitable moment, since you asked for one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, since you say that some of these rocky features were above the line, how did you check that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: We visited some of the old positions which you can still see today along the area of the green line. Below that feature, the ground drops away, but above that feature, or to the north, there are still some features, slightly higher in altitude. We also went up and visited those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to know whether this line belonged to one army or the other -- although by stating that we know that in this area the lines moved considerably?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: These were the features pointed out to me on the ground. So their precise location on a precise day, obviously I am not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We could stop here, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have something to contemplate on for Monday. My learned colleague has put a proposition -- sorry, my learned colleague has included a proposition to the witness, a proposition to the effect that the confrontation line at that point changed frequently. I'd be grateful if my learned colleague on Monday, perhaps, could give the reference for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will give it. That will be a map in colour that we will make copies of, and we have a key which shows perfectly well the evolution of lines, or the change of lines in this area, and we also have the testimony of Mr. Karavelic. Mr. President, I believe that the witness could be thanked for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- I was thinking before I would say something. Mr. Higgs, we have to deal for a couple of minutes with other issues. I do understand that you could return Monday morning at 9.00. It's not sure -- for sure at this very moment that we could start right away at 9.00, but we are aware that it's important for you to leave The Hague by approximately 2.00, and it's the expectation of the Chamber that your testimony will be concluded by then. So you are excused. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Higgs out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This will be extremely difficult to re-organise ourselves for technical reasons, but what my co-counsel is suggesting - I apologise - is that we are trying to hear Mr. Kapetanovic on Monday to start with, first thing in the morning, and then from then on, perhaps, we could hear Witness Higgs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it that the registry will inform the Victims and Witnesses Unit that we do not need the witness right at 9.00 but that an arrival at 10.00 would do. Yes. Then Mr. Ierace, I still owe you an answer to the question of the -- of the witness, why we rejected your objection against the question to the witness why he did not mention any of the areas below the green line. I think that's exactly a matter of methodology. An expert does not just indicate why he finds suitable places for mortars at a certain place, but he also should tell us why he would not find any suitable places in another area he inspected. Because if you do that by examining the expert, you can test the methodology he used. For example, if he would have said, "There were no suitable places because there were so many children playing there that you could not put a mortar there," then someone who would try to test the methodology of the expert could have asked him whether he was sure that at the time of the event there were as many children there as well. I mean, it's just a matter of explaining how you come to your conclusions, not only the positive ones but also the negative ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, his answer was to that effect, but I take it that your concern is that he did not say that in his report, his written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's for what the question -- about whether he did not reflect in his report that he visited the area and why he did not find any suitable locations and on what basis. Then we'll adjourn until next Monday, 9.00. Madam Registrar, I take it in Courtroom II again. Yes. I wish everyone a good weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
